title: Enterprises will eventually run 80% of tokens on open models, but spend only 20% of budget
dek: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will run on open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.
why: The CEO of Ollama gives first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes look nothing alike, and the real constraint on enterprise purchasing is security, not cost.
who: Founders building AI applications and agents, engineers who own enterprise AI procurement and architecture, and investors trying to judge the commercialization path for open models.
skip: The first minute of show intro and the YC recruiting spot at the end are skippable.

points.h: The driver behind open models is control, not saving money
points.body: Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is "better control over AI and customizing it for yourself." Cost is just the piece that can be solved in the short term; only once it is solved does customizing the model to your own use case come up. The order matters: if you treat open models only as a cost-cutting measure, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption onto open models, currently mostly US and European models, while also evaluating Chinese ones.

points.h: Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
points.body: Ollama's per-user token usage curve on the cloud has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could carry a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, customer service, marketing and sales can all hand a hard problem to an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and pulling data along the way, burning enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this surge.

points.h: Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
points.body: Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors ahead of launch, but Jeff says getting a model a few weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work is crammed into the final 24 hours before release. Three things have to land at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, and it has to be fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are plenty of open-source harnesses now, like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the single biggest day of growth. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, inference layer and application runtime all have to be glued together, and it is a combinatorial explosion problem.

points.h: Above the token is where the new scarcity lives
points.body: Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (wiring company data and context into the model), coordination (one request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgment: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B above the token. Following the path of cloud computing, developers will ultimately prefer the best standalone product at every layer rather than something bundled together like Heroku or Google App Engine.

points.h: Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
points.body: Asked whether the harness will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgment is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but a few categories cannot. One is state — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up to the latest data, so storage is a huge standalone problem space. The other is credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole security toolset the way closed providers do, and that is critical to enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

points.h: 80% of tokens run on open models, but only 20% of budget
points.body: Jeff's steady-state judgment: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will run on open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget flows to open source. The open community is driving cost extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spend lands on open models. The hardest work stays with the frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the big middle is done by combining open and closed. He uses a law firm analogy: the partner hands work down to a pile of associates.

points.h: Local and cloud model mixes are not remotely the same
points.body: On local models, US and Chinese models are roughly neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a three-way mix of US, European and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is clear too: coding agents write code and tests, hit many hard problems, and lean mainly on large cloud models; workflows with low end-to-end difficulty like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router deciding when to go up to a large model.

points.h: The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens
points.body: Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, within less than 3 months of the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve was extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually get back to that state, but it requires model architectures trained specifically for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

points.h: Two years without finding the problem is scarier than no hype
points.body: Jeff says that when he entered YC in 2021, the direction he wrote down was "Kitematic for Kubernetes" or "Docker Desktop for Kubernetes," building security products like SSO for Kubernetes. The company entered YC in 2021, and Ollama did not launch until July 2023 — more than two years in between. He says the scariest thing is not whether there is hype, but that "you cannot even see the north star" — customers are usually a good north star, and not being able to see it is scarier. The team was already over 10 people at the time, and he is especially grateful to them for sticking through several pivots.

points.h: First version in two weeks, and Llama 2 launched right on cue
points.body: The trigger for the pivot was an all-hands discussion in Toronto: what would we build if we started from zero today. They saw two problems — one, build a gateway to access any model (framed at the time as Segment for LLMs, the router idea that came later), and two, they were ex-VMware, ex-Docker people who were good at making things run, so make open models run. They gave themselves two weeks to build the first version, and Llama 2 happened to launch right at the end of those two weeks, so they shipped immediately. Jeff calls it bias to action: from idea to launch in two weeks, with more users than all their previous products combined.

points.h: Free and runnable anywhere took a hobbyist tool straight into the Fortune 500
points.body: Jeff says what surprised them most was the speed from hobbyists to the Fortune 500. Two reasons: open models are free to start with, and they can run anywhere — which is extremely important to Fortune 500 IT developer teams, because they do not need to request permission to use them. What is good for hobbyists translated directly into something good for developers inside the enterprise. He draws a database analogy: MongoDB also went from developers to the enterprise, but LLMs are stateless, which makes that transition even easier than for databases.

points.h: The rules of the infrastructure era do not hold in AI
points.body: Jeff gives two pieces of old muscle memory that have to be broken. One is "building a layer on top of someone else is dangerous" — true in the infrastructure era, not true in the AI era, where moving up the stack may actually be better because you are closer to the customer. The other is that in the systems world everything must run exactly as designed, tested and verified, whereas an LLM by definition does not, and that is a feature, not a bug. He also mentions team size: some problems do not need that many people now, such as customer service pipelines, the way cloud services are delivered, and the very fact that "no engineer knows how all the code works."
